title: Timothy Morton
summary: Timothy Morton is a British philosopher who thinks about how to live in an age of ecological crisis. Morton proposes giving up the idea of “Nature” as something distant and separate from us, and acknowledging that we are already entangled with everything living and non-living. This “dark ecology” doesn't promise easy comfort, but it invites you to stay honestly with the anxiety, sadness and strangeness of our situation — and to find an unexpected tenderness in them.
onEmotions: For Morton, feelings are not an obstacle to ecological thinking but its very material. Ecological awareness, in Morton's words, moves from the depressing through the uncanny to the strangely sweet. Anxiety, sadness, guilt and a sense of strangeness are understandable responses to “hyperobjects” — vast phenomena like global warming that can never be seen whole. Morton is skeptical of moralizing and of “dumping information” on people, and believes that guilt that gets stuck is paralyzing. The suggestion is not to jump out of a feeling but to go deeper into it — that is where a connection with other beings is found.

anxiety.text: Anxiety often comes without a clear object — and that is not a sign of weakness. Timothy Morton would say that we live among “hyperobjects”: Morton's name for phenomena so vast in time and space that they can never be seen whole — global warming, plastic in the ocean, radioactive waste. They are “viscous”: they stick to us wherever we are and show up only in fragments — a hot day, a news item, a vague unease. From Morton's point of view, anxiety is a quite accurate response to such things: you are feeling something that really exists, even though you cannot take it in at a glance. This view helps you stop treating anxiety as a malfunction. It doesn't need to be “solved” right away — you can acknowledge that it honestly registers the scale of the world in which we have all ended up together.
anxiety.practice: Write down: what “fragment” of some vast, unsurveyable phenomenon did you feel today? Just name it, without trying to grasp the whole.

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and necessary feeling; it protects us. But Morton notes that in our era fear can be strange: we are afraid not of a predator behind a bush but of something that is already here and at the same time somehow not here. Morton's formula from Hyperobjects — “the end of the world has already occurred” — sounds frightening, but its meaning is unexpectedly comforting. What is meant is the end of the “world” as a cozy stage set, a backdrop against which humans are separate from nature. That backdrop has fallen apart — and with it has gone the need to wait for a single grand catastrophe that will settle everything. From this angle one could say that fear stops being the anticipation of an apocalypse and becomes attention to what is happening now. Living like this does not mean giving up: it means caring for what is near, concrete and real, step by step.
fear.practice: Set aside thoughts of the future for a minute and name three concrete things that surround you right now and that you can take care of.

quote.text: The end of the world has already occurred.
quote.author: Timothy Morton

sadness.text: Sadness in a world where glaciers are melting and species are disappearing is not a whim. Morton calls this approach “dark ecology” and insists that ecological awareness doesn't have to be upbeat and cheerfully green. It is dark — it contains melancholy, an acknowledgment of losses we ourselves take part in. But Morton also describes what happens if you don't run from this darkness: it turns out to have layers. At first it is depressing, then uncanny, and deep down — strangely sweet. Sadness connects you with what you are sad about; it shows that you care. From this angle, to be sad is already to be in a relationship with the world rather than standing apart from it. You can allow yourself sadness not as a dead end but as a door into a deeper connection.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what or whom is this sadness about? Write down one word — and notice that it is something dear to you.

quote.text: Ecological awareness is dark-depressing. Yet it is also dark-uncanny. And strangely, it is dark-sweet.
quote.author: Timothy Morton

grief.text: Grief is one of the most honest feelings: it measures how much what was lost meant to you. Morton writes a great deal about mourning in the ecological age — mourning for species, places, the familiar world — and doesn't try to cut it short. Morton speaks of “the mesh” — the name for the endless interconnectedness of all beings, which has neither center nor edge. From the standpoint of dark ecology one could say that what is gone does not drop out of this mesh without a trace: it goes on being part of what shaped you — in habits, words, a way of looking at the world. Grief doesn't have to “end” on schedule. You can allow it to be slow, as the great natural processes are slow, and notice that mourning is a form of faithfulness to what you loved.
grief.practice: Name one thing, habit or word through which what you lost goes on living in you today.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can feel like being cut off from everyone, and that pain is real. Morton suggests looking at it from an unexpected side. In Humankind Morton speaks of solidarity with “nonhuman people” — animals, plants, even bacteria. You are literally never alone: trillions of microorganisms live in your body, and every breath connects you with trees and algae. Morton calls other beings “strange strangers”: they are close and at the same time never fully knowable — just as we are to ourselves. This does not cancel the longing for human warmth; that longing is legitimate. But perhaps loneliness will soften a little if you notice that you are already surrounded by many presences with whom you can be in quiet solidarity.
loneliness.practice: Find one nonhuman being nearby — a plant, a bird outside the window, a cat — and for a minute simply be near it, asking nothing of it.

anger.text: Anger often points to something that really is unjust. Morton doesn't call for suppressing it, but suggests taking a closer look at where it is directed. Morton describes “agrilogistics” — the agricultural civilization's program, thousands of years old, that seeks to separate humans from the rest of the world and to control everything. Much of what angers us today is the flip side of this program, not only someone's personal villainy. At the same time, Morton is skeptical of an accusatory tone: shouting and shaming, in Morton's view, do a poor job of changing the world. From this angle, anger can be respected as a signal without letting it turn into one more attempt to control everything. Sometimes the strongest thing you can do with anger is turn it into care for something concrete.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly do I want to protect when I'm angry? Write it down in one word.

shame.text: Shame squeezes painfully, as if you had been seen from every side at once. Morton notes that ecological awareness often begins with exactly this kind of awkwardness: you suddenly see yourself as part of a system you didn't choose, and the plastic cup in your hand becomes evidence. But Morton insists that shaming is a poor teacher. In Being Ecological Morton argues: you are already ecological, simply because you exist, breathe, are connected with others. You don't first have to become “good enough” to have the right to be part of the world. From this angle, shame can be taken as a moment when your connectedness with others shows through, not as a verdict. You have been seen — which means you are not separate. That is hard, but it is also where closeness begins.
shame.practice: Put your hand on your chest and say to yourself: “I am already part of this world; I don't need to earn my place.”

guilt.text: Guilt says that the consequences of your actions matter to you — that is a valuable quality. But Morton warns of a trap often seen in ecological conversations: endless guilt is paralyzing. The peculiarity of hyperobjects is that your personal contribution is at once real and statistically negligible: one car trip decides nothing, but billions of trips change the climate. From Morton's point of view one could say that guilt inflated to the scale of the planet quietly puts you at the center of the world — and that is the same old illusion of a separate, all-powerful human. You can turn the volume down: you are one of many threads, not the sole author. Responsibility doesn't have to be self-flagellation; it can be calm, everyday and shared with others.
guilt.practice: Draw two circles: in one, what in this situation really depends on you; in the other, what belongs to large systems.

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but deeply human feeling, and admitting it already takes courage. Morton doesn't write about envy directly, but from the standpoint of this thinking one could say the following. Envy rests on comparing separate, closed-off “selves”: they have it, I don't. Yet Morton keeps showing that the border between “me” and “the other” is far more porous than it seems: we are made of other beings and take part in one “mesh” of interconnections. Moreover, for Morton every thing is more than its visible side — something hidden, inaccessible to the gaze, always remains in it. The life you envy is also more than its facade. This doesn't cancel envy, but it makes it gentler: you are comparing yourself with a picture, not with a living being in all its depth.
envy.practice: Think of someone you envy and finish the sentence: “What I don't know about their life is…”

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be especially heavy: it seems you feel nothing at all. Morton described something similar as part of contemporary experience — a numbness before scale, when alarming news no longer produces anything but a sense of being frozen. Morton doesn't see this as indifference. From this point of view one could say it is a protective response to something too big to digest. Morton is skeptical of attempts to “shake people up” with fresh doses of frightening facts and suggests another path — paying attention to small things: texture, sound, the strangeness of ordinary objects. In Morton's philosophy even the simplest thing, a drop or a stone, is inexhaustible and mysterious. You don't have to fill the emptiness by force; it is enough to let the small world become noticeable again, one detail at a time.
emptiness.practice: Pick up any object near you and for a minute examine it as if seeing it for the first time. What turned out to be strange about it?

confusion.text: Feeling lost is a natural state when the familiar maps stop working. Morton considers it not a mistake but an honest response to our age. Hyperobjects, in Morton's words, are “nonlocal” and “phased”: we see only separate slices of phenomena that unfold on scales beyond the eye's reach — as if a three-dimensional shape were passing through a flat plane. So losing your bearings is not your personal inability to understand but an accurate reflection of the situation. Morton generally values “the uncanny” — the feeling when something familiar suddenly becomes strange. For Morton this is the beginning of a truer view: the world was always stranger than we thought. From this angle, confusion can be accepted as curiosity without a ready answer. You don't have to know right away what is going on; you can live in the question for a while.
confusion.practice: Write down a question that is confusing you right now, and leave it unanswered until evening — just as a question.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are a signal that you have been carrying more than you can for a long time. Speaking of ecology, Morton notes that what exhausts us is not only the problem itself but also a certain way of talking about it: as a nonstop emergency, where mountains of facts are dumped on people and an immediate reaction is expected. Morton calls this “info-dump mode” and believes that it makes no one either wiser or kinder. From Morton's point of view one could say that endless rushing repeats the very logic that led to the crisis: speed everything up, control everything. Rest, therefore, is not betrayal. It can be a form of ecological existence: slowing down, the way trees slow down in winter. You too are part of the living world, which has rhythms and a right to pause.
fatigue.practice: Choose one thing that you can skip today or do more slowly. Allow yourself this without explanations.

boredom.text: Boredom seems a small feeling, but it says a lot about how we relate to the world. From Morton's point of view one could say that boredom arises when the world turns into a “background” — a neutral stage set where nothing happens. It is precisely the idea of background that Morton argues against. In Ecology without Nature Morton shows that “nature” as a calm backdrop for human affairs is an illusion. In reality, life is teeming all around: mycelium under the asphalt, microbes in the air, the slow work of stone and water. Every thing, for Morton, is inexhaustible: it can never be known completely. So boredom is not a verdict on the world but an invitation to change scale. It can become the beginning of attentiveness if you let yourself linger on what seems boring.
boredom.practice: Look at the most boring spot in the room — a corner, a wall, a windowsill — and find three things there that are living their own lives.

joy.text: Joy in hard times can seem out of place — as if you are not allowed to be glad when the world is in trouble. Morton thinks otherwise. In Dark Ecology Morton writes that at the depths of ecological awareness lies something sweet, and the later books speak more and more of play and pleasure as a full part of ecological life. Morton notes that a relationship with the world built only on duty and fear quickly runs out of breath. From this angle, joy is not an escape from problems but one of the ways of being connected with other beings: joy at the smell of rain or a cat's purring already links you with the nonhuman world. You can allow yourself joy without guilt — it too is part of caring for life.
joy.practice: Recall which nonhuman being or phenomenon made you glad recently — and silently say thank you to it.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the strongest confirmations that we are not alone. Morton widens the circle of love further than we are used to. In Humankind Morton proposes solidarity with “nonhuman people” and insists that a feeling of closeness to animals, plants, even to things, is not sentimentality but an accurate perception of reality. Morton speaks of the “strange stranger”: a beloved being always remains somewhat unknowable, and that is precisely where its aliveness lies. From this angle, tenderness is not possession but a willingness to be near someone you don't fully understand. This can remove some of the anxiety in love: you don't need to know another completely in order to love them. It is enough to respect their mystery and stay close.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name one trait of theirs that remains a mystery to you. Let it simply be.

gratitude.text: Gratitude comes when we notice that life does not rest on us alone. Morton helps us see how literally true this is. Everything you do, you do together with others: the mitochondria in your cells were once separate bacteria, oxygen was produced by plants and algae, bread was grown by soil, sun and many people. Morton calls this interconnectedness “the mesh,” which has no center and no edge. From the standpoint of dark ecology, gratitude is not mere politeness but a sober acknowledgment of dependence. And this dependence is not a humiliation but a form of belonging. To give thanks is to see yourself as a knot in a vast fabric of life that no one created alone and that, despite everything, goes on.
gratitude.practice: Choose one thing you ate or drank today and trace at least three links — people and beings — thanks to whom it reached you.

hope.text: Hope in a time of crisis can be fragile, and it is normal to doubt it. Morton suggests not confusing hope with waiting to be rescued. Morton notes that apocalyptic thinking — “everything is about to collapse” or “we are about to be saved” — itself leads us away from the present. When Morton says that the end of the world has already occurred, the point is that it is time to stop waiting for the finale and start living inside what is. Hope then becomes not a belief in a happy ending but a trust in a future that is truly open and not yet written. And since it is unknown, there is room in it for the unexpected. You can hope modestly — for the next step, for a neighbor, for spring — and that is enough.
hope.practice: Write down one small thing you are hoping for in the coming week. Just one, and just a small one.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for what once was, and there is a lot of tenderness in it. Morton treats it attentively and a little critically. Morton shows that many of our images of “untouched nature” and “the good old days” are romantic constructions, a pastoral picture that never existed in pure form. At the same time, longing for a home that is changing is real. Here a term from the Australian philosopher Glenn Albrecht is fitting — “solastalgia”: the pain of changes in the place where you still live, homesickness without ever leaving home. From Morton's point of view one could say that nostalgia is worth accepting without turning it into a program for returning to an ideal past. Let memory make you gentler with the present: what you miss hints at what is worth protecting now.
nostalgia.practice: Name exactly what you miss — and find in today at least a tiny echo of it.

craving.text: A sharp craving — “I want it right now” — can be almost unbearable, and there is nothing shameful in that. Morton likes the image of a loop: dark ecology, in Morton's words, is shaped like a loop in which we come back to the same place again and again and each time see it a little differently. From the standpoint of this thinking one could say that craving moves in loops too: it rises, peaks and ebbs, and then may return. Morton doesn't suggest leaping out of the loop in a single jerk — the suggestion is to notice its shape. Each time you see the wave from the side, you are already inside it a little differently. The craving is not the whole of you, but one of the many beings and processes you are made of.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, watch it like the weather: where is it in your body, is it growing, is it changing? Note the moment when it starts to ebb, even slightly.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a cycle that can be very hard not to fall into and hard to get out of. Morton describes “agrilogistics” — the millennia-old program of agricultural civilization, which once helped people survive and later began to run almost automatically, even to our harm. From the standpoint of dark ecology one could say that addiction resembles such a program on a small scale: something that once brought relief or protection gradually organized a whole life around itself. Morton doesn't blame people for agrilogistics, but shows how such programs capture everyone. And Morton believes in solidarity: we are not separate atoms but part of a mesh of connections. Getting out of the cycle is easier together, too.
addiction.practice: Ask yourself: what did the thing my life is now built around once protect me from, or make easier? If you'd like, you can talk this over with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after can be hard: your body aches, and anxiety, shame and fragments of memory arrive. That is understandable, and it doesn't make you any worse. Morton writes that hyperobjects are “viscous”: the more we learn about them, the more they stick to us. From this angle one could say that a hangover is viscous too: last night seems stuck to this morning. Morton suggests neither tearing this stickiness away in disgust nor drowning in guilt — guilt that gets stuck, Morton believes, is paralyzing. Instead you can simply acknowledge: yes, I am here, inside this morning, with my body. Dark ecology begins when you stop pretending you are standing outside.
hangover.practice: Drink some water slowly, feeling each sip. Tell yourself: “It's morning now, and I'm taking care of my body” — without judging last night.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria can be wonderful, and there is no need to spoil it with suspicion. Morton says that ecological awareness eventually arrives at something “dark-sweet”: a strange joy that we are connected with everything living and non-living. Morton generally considers pleasure and play part of ecological thought, not an obstacle to it. From this angle one could say that euphoria is a moment when the world suddenly seems open and you feel your connectedness with it very keenly. Morton would add that everything in the world oscillates and changes, and a high doesn't last forever either. That doesn't devalue it. You can enjoy it, knowing it is part of a wider rhythm.
euphoria.practice: Notice what exactly seems so alive right now: the light, a sound, a person beside you. Describe this one detail to yourself so as to remember it.

crash.text: The drop after a high can be very painful — as if someone had switched off the light. Many people know this. Morton describes the path of ecological awareness like this: first it is “dark-depressing,” then “uncanny,” and only then “dark-sweet.” Morton doesn't try to leap over the first step — on the contrary, it has to be gone through, not around. From this angle one could say that the comedown is not a malfunction and not proof that the joy was false. It is one of the phases of a wave. Morton suggests not fleeing the dark but going deeper into it: deep in the darkness, in Morton's thinking, something unexpectedly soft is found. For now it is enough simply to let the slump be.
crash.practice: Name three small things that are near you right now and don't change with your mood: a chair, a cup, the light from the window.

panic.text: Panic is very frightening: a wave of terror, your heart and breathing seeming to slip out of control. You are not alone in this, and such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Morton describes “the uncanny” — the feeling when something familiar suddenly becomes alien and threatening, and you cannot step outside because you are inside what is happening. From the standpoint of this thinking one could say that panic is experienced in just this way. But Morton reminds us that you are always surrounded by other beings and things that hold you: the floor, the air, the wall. There is support, even when you can't feel it. Right now you don't need to understand anything — only breathe and notice the support.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel how the floor holds you. Take a few breaths with a long exhale and name out loud five objects around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” a sense of the abyss — is one of the heaviest feelings, and Morton doesn't try to cancel it. Morton writes about hyperobjects — phenomena so vast in time and space that a human life beside them seems tiny. It is the encounter with them that brings that chill of the abyss. But Morton insists that the “dark” and the “uncanny” are not necessarily followed by despair. There, in Morton's words, a strange sweetness is found: we are not alone before the abyss; we are entangled with countless beings who also live, breathe and endure. From this angle, the answer to “what for” is not a formula but a connection that is already there.
dread.practice: Choose one living being near you — a plant, a bird outside the window, a person — and for a minute simply be in its company, noting that you are both here.

fomo.text: The feeling that you are not where you should be while everyone else lives more interesting lives is very common. Morton can offer an unexpected view. Morton insists that “Nature” as a special faraway place where everything is authentic does not exist: we are already inside everything there is. One could put it this way: there is no “real life” somewhere out there either. The feed shows other people's bright snapshots, but life, for Morton, is a mesh of connections without a center. In the mesh there is no “main place” with a better view. Where you are right now, an endless amount of strange and interesting things is also intertwined — it just isn't packaged into a picture. You can notice the fear of missing out and gently bring your attention back here.
fomo.practice: Look around and find one thing in your space that has something strange or surprising about it if you look closely. Describe it in one sentence.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and thoughts at three in the morning are exhausting, and not being able to fall asleep is not your fault. At night everything seems bigger, scarier, more final. Morton writes a great deal about different scales of time: alongside human days and nights run the slow rhythms of stones, trees, stars. From this angle one could say that at three in the morning you are not left alone with your anxiety: all around you a vast, unhurried life goes on that needs none of your decisions right now. Morton suggests “attuning” to the world around you, as to music. You can try attuning to the quiet sounds of the night instead of the endless circle of thoughts.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, listen for three different night sounds — a hum, breathing, noise outside the window. Focus on one of them for a few exhales.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: trust collapses, and the world seems less reliable. This pain is legitimate. Morton writes about the “strange stranger” — Morton's name for any other being: the closer we are to someone, the clearer it becomes that we don't fully know them. From this angle one could say that betrayal is a painful encounter with this unknowability of the other. That doesn't make you naive: to trust is to open yourself to someone who can never be fully known, and it is the only way to be close. Morton doesn't call on you to stop trusting. The suggestion is to acknowledge that the bond was always fragile, and that your openness was courage, not a mistake.
betrayal.practice: Write down: “I trusted because…” Note which good quality of yours stood behind that trust.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is tormenting, and behind it there is often a fear of losing someone very dear. Morton speaks of the “strange stranger”: even the person closest to us remains not fully knowable; they have depths that are closed to us. From this angle one could say that jealousy is anxiety before this opacity: a wish to know and hold on to the other completely. But for Morton the unknowability of the other is not a threat but part of what makes them alive and interesting. No one can be made entirely yours, and that is not your failure. You can acknowledge jealousy and notice that there is tenderness behind it, not only fear.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: “What do I love in this person that I cannot control?” Write down one such trait.

resentment.text: An old grudge is heavy: you carry it for years, and it is understandable — you really were hurt. Morton writes that hyperobjects are “viscous”: they stick, and you can't step back to a safe distance from them. From the standpoint of this thinking one could say that a grudge is viscous too — it sticks to your life and trails after you. Morton doesn't suggest tearing it off abruptly: Morton is generally against gestures that promise quick purification. But Morton shows that viscosity is not the whole picture. In the mesh of connections you live in, there are many other threads besides this one. You can acknowledge the grudge and gradually give your attention to the threads that nourish you.
resentment.practice: Name three connections in your life — with people, places, activities — that have nothing to do with this grudge. Spend a minute with one of them.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically, and that pain speaks of how deeply you were connected. Morton believes that a connection doesn't simply vanish: in “the mesh,” Morton's name for the endless entanglement of beings, nothing drops out without a trace. From this angle one could say that a breakup changes the form of the connection but doesn't erase how you changed each other. Morton also insists that sadness is not a mistake but a form of attunement to the world: we grieve because we are able to feel others. Dark ecology doesn't hurry grief or demand that you “let go” by a certain date. You can let your heart ache and at the same time notice that you are still connected to much else.
heartbreak.practice: Put your palm on your chest and feel its warmth. Tell yourself: “It hurts because it mattered.”

impostor.text: The fear of being found out is familiar to a great many people — including those you admire. Morton offers an unexpectedly comforting view. In Morton's philosophy no thing fully coincides with itself: everything is a little “strange,” everything has hidden depths that never come to the surface. Even a stone, for Morton, is more than the way it appears to us. From this angle one could say that no one is ever “the real thing” in the ideal sense you expect of yourself. Everyone is a little out of step with their roles. Feeling like an impostor is not proof that you are a fraud, but a sign that you, like everything in the world, are larger and more complex than any role.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you really did well, without the caveat “but that was luck.”

self_hatred.text: The inner critic can sound merciless, but its verdict is not the truth about you. Morton compares ecological awareness to noir — a detective story in which the investigator suddenly discovers that they are implicated in the crime. But Morton insists that this discovery shouldn't lead to self-flagellation: guilt that gets stuck, in Morton's view, paralyzes and fixes nothing. Dark ecology accepts the dark, the unlovely and the strange — in everything, including ourselves. From this angle one could say: the darkness you see in yourself does not make you unworthy. Everything alive is imperfect and entangled, and you deserve the same tenderness as the rest of the world.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase of your inner critic. Then write next to it what you would say to a friend who talked about themselves that way.

helplessness.text: Being powerless to change something is hard, and it often reflects the real scale of the circumstances. Morton knows this feeling well: hyperobjects like global warming are so vast that one person's action seems negligible. Morton doesn't pretend otherwise. But Morton proposes the concept of “subscendence”: the whole, in Morton's formula, is always less than the sum of its parts, so each part is not dissolved in the whole and keeps its significance. From this angle one could say that your small action does not dissolve in the vast. It is real, even if it doesn't change everything. And you are not alone: helplessness before the vast is a shared feeling, and what is shared is easier to bear.
helplessness.practice: Choose one tiny task that is within your power today. Do it and note: “this really happened.”

quote.text: Hyperobjects are things that are massively distributed in time and space relative to humans.
quote.author: Timothy Morton

procrastination.text: When you can't get started, it is usually not laziness but tiredness, fear, or the feeling that the task is too heavy to lift. In Being Ecological Morton notes that we are paralyzed by the idea that everything has to be done perfectly and all at once — and that a flood of guilt and alarming facts only gets in the way of acting. Morton says that in a sense we are already ecological, rather than having to become perfect first. From this angle one could say: you don't have to become “the right kind of person” first in order to begin. You can start with an imperfect, small, almost playful step. Morton generally values play and lightness as a way into what is difficult.
procrastination.practice: Do the smallest, even silly, part of the task — open the file, write one word. Allow it to be imperfect.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — a move, emigration, losing the ground under your feet — is a real loss. Morton criticizes the idea that we each have one “natural” place where we belong, like a plant in a garden bed. For Morton, the connections between beings are arranged like a mesh with neither center nor edge. From this angle one could say that, having lost a familiar place, you do not fall out of the world: you are still in the mesh; its threads are simply weaving together in a new way. Morton doesn't devalue homesickness — Morton understands how much places and attachments matter. But Morton shows that belonging is not only roots in a single spot but also connections that can be tied anew.
uprooted.practice: In the new place, find one being or thing — a tree, a bird, a smell — that reminds you of home or that you simply like. Greet it in your mind.

overload.text: Overload from an endless feed and informational noise is exhausting, and it is an understandable response to your environment, not a weakness of yours. Morton directly criticizes the “info dump” — the habit of pouring more and more alarming facts on people in the hope that they will change. In Morton's view this doesn't help; it only deafens and paralyzes. Morton offers something else: instead of absorbing everything, attuning to a little — to what is near, to a specific thing, sound, being. From this angle one could say that getting tired of the stream is normal. You are not obliged to hold the whole world inside you at once. Sometimes the most ecological thing is to put the phone down and notice what is right in front of you.
overload.practice: Put your phone down for two minutes and describe to yourself one thing you see — its color, shape, texture — in as much detail as you can.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle treatment. Morton, associated with object-oriented ontology, argues precisely that reality is strange: no thing is given to us whole; each has depths hidden from us, and the way things appear is always a little different from what they are. From this angle one could say that a feeling of unreality is a heightened experience of this ordinary strangeness. The world has not disappeared — it has simply shown its unfamiliar side for a moment. Morton suggests not being frightened of the strange, but gently touching concrete things.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object with a distinct texture and describe three of its qualities to yourself: weight, temperature, shape.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling, worth simply living through. Morton reflects a great deal on the sublime. From the standpoint of this thinking one could say that awe is a moment when something vast and alien suddenly touches you: the night sky, the ocean, an ancient tree. Morton is drawn less to the idea of the sublime as reason's victory over the elements than to a sense of an intimate encounter with what is larger and older than us. It is not about mastering the vast, but about letting it come close. Your awe is a sign that you are open to a world that holds far more than it seems.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute, doing nothing. Notice how your body responds to it.

relief.text: Relief is a quiet and important feeling, and you can let it be there fully. Morton often speaks of how hard it is to constantly carry anxiety and guilt, as if the whole world rested on your shoulders. From the standpoint of dark ecology one could say that relief is a moment when you notice: the world does not rest on you alone. All around there are many beings and processes doing their work: the air, the earth, other people. Morton believes that lightness and even pleasure are not a betrayal of seriousness but part of how we can be connected with the world. You can simply live through relief without hurrying on to the next worry.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body things got lighter. Think about who or what else helps hold your world up.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and you don't have to earn it. In Ecology without Nature Morton writes a great deal about “the ambient” — the background, the surroundings, the sound of the world that usually goes unnoticed. Morton compares it to ambient music, which doesn't demand strained attention but simply surrounds you. From this angle one could say that calm is a moment when you begin to hear this background: the quiet presence of things that exist beside you with no purpose at all. Calm is not emptiness but attunement to the world. You can simply be in it, without turning it into a task and without asking how long it will last — the world goes on sounding even when you aren't listening.
calm.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and listen to the background: the quietest sounds around you. Let them simply sound.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the joyful sense that something new has suddenly become possible. In Realist Magic Morton argues that causality is aesthetic in nature: things influence one another the way a melody influences a listener. From this angle one could say that inspiration is not only your personal achievement but an encounter: something in the world — an image, a sound, a being, an idea — touched you and set off a response. You don't create alone; you answer. Morton values this approach to creativity: not as conquering material, but as attuning to what arrives. You can simply open yourself to inspiration and gratefully notice who and what took part in it along with you.
inspiration.practice: Write down what exactly inspired you — an image, a sound, a phrase. Then write down one thought that answers it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is awkward to admit, but it happens to almost everyone: someone stumbles, and for a moment something inside feels pleased. Morton doesn't write about schadenfreude directly, but from the standpoint of this thinking one could say the following. Morton describes “agrilogistics” — the logic by which humanity has built its life for millennia: fence yourself off, win, survive at others' expense. Schadenfreude is a small echo of that logic: another's failure seems to confirm that we are safe. At the same time, Morton loves the comic and notes that ecological awareness resembles comedy: all of us keep tripping over our own consequences. From this angle, laughter at someone else's fall can be turned around: we are not spectators but fellow participants in this shared stumbling. Then schadenfreude can soften into a sympathetic smile.
schadenfreude.practice: Recall a time recently when you yourself “stumbled” in the same way. Look at the two situations side by side — what changed in the feeling?

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of purity: I'm not like that, I stand apart. It is an understandable defense, especially when something has hurt you. In Ecology without Nature Morton criticizes the position Hegel called the “beautiful soul” — the stance of someone who condemns a corrupt world as if standing outside it, implicated in nothing. Morton shows that no such “outside” exists: we are all entangled in a shared “mesh” of connections. From this angle one could say that contempt is an attempt to step out of the mesh and look down on others. It brings relief, but it also isolates. Morton suggests not canceling your judgment but going back inside: acknowledging that both I and the one I despise are parts of the same tangled situation. From that point it is easier to see what really hurt you.
contempt.practice: Finish the sentence: “I despise this because I'm afraid of turning out to be…”. Notice that the answer says something about you, not about the other person.

disgust.text: Disgust is an ancient bodily reaction: to recoil, not to touch. It can arise toward people, situations and yourself, and no one chooses it. Morton thinks a great deal about the disgusting. Morton believes that ecological thought loved only beautiful “Nature” for too long — mountains, sunsets — and turned away from slime, rot, garbage, from what sticks. Hyperobjects, for Morton, are “viscous”: they stick to us, and we can't wash them off. And our own body is made up of countless bacteria and other beings — the border of the “self” is far more porous than we'd like to think. From this angle, disgust is a reaction to a blurred boundary. Morton suggests not fighting it but noticing it and staying nearby: the world, and we ourselves, don't have to be clean to deserve attention.
disgust.practice: Name the boundary that the disgust is guarding. Say to yourself: “I don't have to be clean in order to be alive.”

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is usually born of pain and a sense of injustice. This feeling has the right to be heard. Morton doesn't write about revenge directly, but Morton has an important figure — the “loop.” Morton shows how human attempts to eliminate a threat once and for all often come back to us in a new form: we act, and the consequences loop around. From this angle one could say that revenge promises to settle the score but in fact more often starts a new loop in which you remain tied to the person who hurt you. Morton doesn't moralize, simply noting that in an entangled world there is no clean, final return blow. Admitting the wish for revenge is honest. And behind it there usually stands something else: a wish for your pain to be acknowledged, and to feel safe again.
revenge.practice: Write down what would have to happen for you to feel safe. Note which parts of it depend on you.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people closest to us can be the most searing, and afterward we feel ashamed of it. That doesn't make you a bad person. Morton speaks of the “strange stranger”: the closer we come to another being, the stranger and more unpredictable it turns out to be. Closeness doesn't make the other more understandable — it makes them even more mysterious. From this angle one could say that anger at a partner, parent or child is born precisely of closeness: you are so tightly entangled that every difference feels like a blow. In Morton's “mesh” there is no safe distance between those who are connected. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't cancel love either. It points to a place where your lives are woven especially tight — and where more air, or a conversation, may be needed.
anger_at_loved.practice: Take a few slow exhales and ask yourself: what in me has been touched right now — tiredness, fear, loneliness?

ambivalence.text: Loving and not being able to stand the same person is hard, and it seems as though one of the feelings must be false. Morton disagrees. Morton believes that things and beings are contradictory by their very nature: they are themselves and at the same time do not coincide with how they are given to us. Morton even writes sympathetically about a logic that allows something to be both one thing and the other at once. And Morton criticizes “agrilogistics,” the old logic of control, precisely for its drive to eliminate all contradiction. From this angle one could say that mixed feelings toward someone close are not a mistake but an honest reflection of the fact that they are complex — as you are. You don't need to pick one feeling and throw away the other. You can let them both be.
ambivalence.practice: Put it into one sentence: “I love you, and…”. Don't correct it — just read it.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after someone leaves, or after the death of a gravely ill loved one often comes with guilt: how can I feel relief if I loved them? Morton describes ecological awareness as a path through the “dark-depressing,” the “dark-uncanny” and the “dark-sweet” — in Morton's work feelings are never pure; they are mixed and layered. From this angle one could say that relief and grief don't contradict each other but live in the same fabric. Relief doesn't cancel love: it speaks of how long you carried the weight — the fear, the care, the strain. Morton is generally distrustful of guilt that gets stuck and paralyzes. You don't have to choose which feeling is the “right” one. You can let relief be, and let love stay beside it.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: “I feel relief, and I love.” Notice where in your body each of these parts responds.

indifference.text: Sometimes something “should” move you, but inside there is silence, and that feels awkward. Morton is very attentive to this state. Morton writes that hyperobjects — vast phenomena like global warming — can never be felt as a whole: they are too big, stretched out across time and space. So numbness is a natural reaction of the human psyche, not a moral defect. Morton also criticizes the “info dump”: a flood of grim facts doesn't awaken feelings but rather dulls them. From this angle one could say that indifference often turns out to be overload rather than emptiness. Morton suggests not forcing yourself to feel, but starting with what is small and near: with what you can see, hear, touch. A feeling that isn't ordered to appear sometimes comes back on its own.
indifference.practice: Find something alive near you — a plant, a bird, your own breathing — and watch it for a minute, expecting nothing.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — is understandable when life has become cramped. Morton likes to remind us that in the ecological age “there is no ‘away’”: when we throw something away, it doesn't vanish; it simply ends up somewhere else in the same world. You could hear this as a reproach, but in Morton it is more of a comfort. From this angle one could say that leaving doesn't take you out of the world, but it can change your position in the “mesh” of connections — and that is a very real change. And also: wherever you go, you won't end up outside your connection with others. Morton gives no advice on whether to leave or stay. But Morton does invite you to ask yourself which threads you'd like to loosen and which you would take with you.
escape.practice: Draw three threads you'd like to be free of, and three you would take with you anywhere.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to an unavailable or “wrong” person can be unsettling: as if something were pulling you against your will. Drawing on object-oriented ontology, Morton holds that every thing and every being is always more than what we can see: a hidden depth remains in it. In Realist Magic Morton describes how things act on one another almost aesthetically — enchanting, attracting, as in music or art. From this angle one could say that attraction is one form of this pull: something in another person resonates in you, and you didn't choose it. The attraction itself is neither an act nor a verdict. Morton passes no moral judgments, suggesting instead that you look gently at what exactly draws you so strongly.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down three words about what draws you to this person. Which of them could become part of your own life?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can grip you so tightly that it's hard to raise your eyes. This is a very common feeling. Morton speaks of the “strange stranger”: every being is mysterious to us, and the better we get to know it, the stranger it becomes. And from the standpoint of object-oriented ontology, no one sees another person whole: a hidden depth always remains in each of us. From this angle one could say that the fear of being judged rests on the illusion that others see right through you. But they see only a small part of you, just as you see only a small part of them. We are all strange strangers to one another, and everyone in the room is a little awkward. This doesn't cancel the nervousness, but it makes it less lonely.
social_anxiety.practice: When you're among people, pick one person and think: “They may be nervous too.” Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is unsettling: it's unclear what will happen, and there's nothing to lean on. Morton believes this feeling accurately reflects our time. Hyperobjects, in Morton's words, are “nonlocal” and “phased”: we never see them whole, only fragments that surface here and there. To live alongside them is to live with incomplete knowledge. Morton proposes bringing hesitation, doubt and even irony back into thinking — not as weakness but as honesty before a complex world. From this angle one could say that uncertainty is not your personal failure but a shared condition of the era that everyone is in. The task is not to get rid of it but to learn to live in it: to do what is visible one step ahead, without demanding the full picture.
uncertainty.practice: Write down what you know for sure right now — even something simple: “I'm breathing,” “today is Tuesday.” Lean on that.

waiting.text: Waiting for results, an answer or news stretches time out, and it feels as if life has been put on pause. This is a hard state. Morton distinguishes two kinds of future: the predictable one — a continuation of what is already known — and the truly open one, which cannot be calculated in advance. In Morton's thinking, the real future is always a little “strange”: it doesn't arrive the way we pictured it. From this angle, waiting is living beside something that has not yet taken shape. The imagination rushes to fill the void with worst-case scenarios, but the future is under no obligation to repeat them. Morton also brings us back to what is happening now: the weather outside the window, the beings around us. While the answer hasn't come, the present hasn't stopped.
waiting.practice: Look out the window and describe the weather to yourself in as much detail as you can. This is what is happening while you wait.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. Morton describes ecological awareness through the plot of a noir: a detective investigates a crime and discovers that they are implicated in it. This is like regret: you suddenly see how your own action played a part. But Morton warns that guilt that gets stuck paralyzes and helps nothing. Morton's loop also works in the other direction: since we are inside events, we can step into them again, a little differently. From this angle one could say that regret is a moment of recognizing yourself in the plot, not a verdict. You don't fall out of the story; you are still in it, and the next turn of the loop can be different.
regret.practice: Write down: “Back then I didn't know…” and “Now I know…”. Note one small action that follows from the second sentence.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person hurts especially sharply: it is precisely them you are missing. Drawing on object-oriented ontology, Morton says that even when they are near, another person is never given to us whole: something hidden and inaccessible always remains in them. Longing makes this truth tangible — but it also shows how deeply they are woven into you. In Humankind Morton writes about the “spectral”: everything around us carries traces of others, and presence is never pure. From this angle one could say that the person you long for goes on being present in you as a thread in the shared “mesh” — in habits, words, a way of seeing the world. Absence doesn't cancel the connection, and longing is one of its forms.
longing.practice: Notice one of your habits or pet phrases that came from this person. Allow yourself to smile at this trace.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from wars, disasters, injustice — can be almost unbearable. It says that you feel your connection with others, even distant ones. Morton writes that we live in an age when enormous events intrude on everyday life, and that the natural responses to this are sadness, anxiety, numbness. Morton is against pouring ever new streams of information over yourself: it doesn't make us stronger, it only drains us. Morton describes the path of feeling: from the depressing through the uncanny to the strangely sweet. From this angle one could say that there is no need to drive away pain for the world — deep within it, solidarity is found, a tenderness toward what is fragile and alive. It is easier to carry when you share it with others and choose small, nearby actions.
world_pain.practice: Set the news aside for an hour. Do one small act of care — for a person, an animal, a plant near you.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts, and it feels as if you have been refused entirely, in everything you are. Morton offers a view that may soften this pain a little. For Morton every being is a “strange stranger,” whose depth is hidden even from itself. The other person also lives by inner laws you cannot see, and their “no” is born of that depth. From this angle one could say that rejection is the meeting of two hidden worlds that didn't match, not a verdict on your worth. Besides, no single gaze takes you in fully: the person who turned you down saw only a part. You are more than what was rejected.
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: “What this person didn't know about me is…”. List three things that are in you.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can sit in the body for a long time, and there is nothing shameful in it. Morton shows that no being is self-sufficient: all of us are held up by others — people, animals, bacteria, air. To be “ecological,” in Morton's words, means precisely to be dependent and connected. From this angle one could say that the fear of being left is not weakness but a keen experience of a fundamental truth: we need one another. But the same thought also brings comfort. Your life hangs not on a single thread but on many connections in the shared “mesh.” If one weakens, the others go on holding you, even if they are hard to notice right now.
abandonment.practice: Write down five threads that are holding you right now: people, places, activities, beings. Look at the whole list.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is the force of a feeling with no answer, and it wears you out. Morton writes a great deal about solidarity with those who cannot answer us in kind in our language: animals, trees, all that is nonhuman. Morton shows that a connection can be asymmetrical and still be real. Of course, with people it is different: we want reciprocity, and its absence hurts. But from this angle one could say that your feeling is neither a mistake nor a failure. It reveals how deeply you are able to be touched by another being. Morton suggests not jumping out of a difficult feeling but staying in it: in time, what is dark in it can become quiet and almost tender.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has revealed to you about yourself. Let it be one line.

humiliation.text: Humiliation causes deep pain: someone tried to put you lower than you are. You have a right to this pain. In Hyperobjects Morton plays on a kinship of words: humiliation, humility and humus (“soil”) share a single root. Morton writes that hyperobjects “bring us down to earth,” and that this is not a disgrace but a return to reality common to everyone. From this angle two experiences can be told apart: the humiliation that people inflict, wanting to diminish you, and the groundedness that simply reminds us that we are all fragile beings among others. The first says something about those who humiliated you. The second takes no dignity away but gives support: standing on the earth, you cannot fall any lower.
humiliation.practice: Put both feet on the floor, feel the support and say: “I'm on the ground. No one can push me off from here.”

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and it doesn't make you shallow. Morton criticizes the idea of “Nature” with a capital N — a beautiful picture, separate from us, that the real world never lives up to. Models of the “correct” body work in a similar way: they are an ideal picture against which the living is compared. From this angle one could say that the body is not a picture but, as Morton stresses, a symbiotic community: billions of other beings live in it; it breathes, changes, intertwines with the world. It was not made to match a model. Morton doesn't suggest forcing yourself to love your body — only noticing that judging it by a picture is as strange as judging a forest by a postcard.
body_shame.practice: Place your palm on your belly or chest and feel how your body breathes on its own, without your control. Stay like this for a minute.

illness.text: Illness, when the body lets you down, is frightening and exhausting, and you have every right to be angry and sad. Morton suggests seeing the body not as a machine we own but as a living community: it is made up of many other beings and constantly depends on the surrounding world. Illness makes this entanglement visible and painfully tangible: you suddenly see that the body doesn't obey orders. From this angle one could say that illness doesn't throw you out of life but shows its fragile side, one we all share. Morton says that being ecological means being vulnerable together with others. In this vulnerability there is also room for tenderness toward yourself: your body is not betraying you; it is doing what it can.
illness.practice: Say one kind sentence to your body, as you would to a tired friend: for example, “You're trying. I'm with you.”

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and you can enjoy it. Morton often argues with a way of thinking in which there is always “not enough”: not enough done, not done right enough. Morton believes such thinking rests on stuck guilt and is paralyzing. In Being Ecological Morton argues that even small actions are real and matter, and in Humankind speaks of the value of joy and play. From this angle one could say that healthy pride is an antidote to the endless “too little.” You did something, and it really happened in the world, leaving a trace in the shared “mesh.” It didn't have to be done perfectly for you to be glad. Allow yourself to linger in this feeling.
pride.practice: Tell someone, or write down for yourself, what you did. Don't add a “but” at the end of the sentence.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet, tender feeling that doesn't need fixing. Morton considers melancholy one of the most honest ecological moods. In Ecology without Nature Morton contrasts it with completed mourning: mourning seeks to let go of what was lost and move on, while melancholy keeps holding it close, staying with what has gone or is going. For Morton there is an ethics in this: not turning away from losses, not pretending that everything can be replaced. From this angle one could say that your gentle sadness is faithfulness to what was precious and a sensitivity to the fragility of the world. Morton describes how a strange sweetness shows through a dark feeling. Melancholy is exactly that kind of sweetness: sad, but full of connection.
melancholy.practice: Spend a few minutes with this mood — by a window or with quiet music. Ask: what does it keep me connected to?
